meta.title: Hawker centre guide: which centre for which dish, and how to behave | Five Foot Way
meta.description: Where to eat chicken rice, laksa, satay and nasi lemak, when the stalls open and close, the tissue-packet rule, returning your tray, and what the UNESCO listing actually means.

hero.title: The hawker centre guide
hero.sub: Which centre for which dish, when to go, and the small courtesies that make you look like you belong.

statement.text: Hawker centres are Singapore's shared dining rooms: covered, open-sided halls where dozens of small family stalls cook one or two dishes each, and where a judge and a delivery rider might share the same table. They are cheap, fast, fan-cooled and, at their best, as good as anything in the city.

unesco.title: What the UNESCO listing means
text: In December 2020, UNESCO added **Hawker Culture in Singapore** to its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. That is a list of living practices, such as crafts, festivals and food traditions, not of buildings. What was recognised is not a particular hall or a particular dish, but the whole culture: the hawkers and their skills, the recipes passed between generations, and the habit of eating together across every community in the city.

The story behind it is practical. Street hawkers once cooked on the pavements of the old town. From the late 1960s to the 1980s, the government moved them into purpose-built centres with running water, drainage and licences, close to public housing. That decision kept cooked food cheap and close to home for most Singaporeans.

The listing comes with a worry: many hawkers are now in their sixties and seventies, the work is long and hot, and fewer children want to take over. Choosing a family stall, being patient in the queue and returning your tray are small ways to support a culture that is being actively protected.

centres.title: Which centre for which dish
centres.text: Our short list, by neighbourhood. Hours below describe the centre as a whole; every stall keeps its own hours and rest days, and popular stalls sell out. Use it as a starting point, not a timetable.

items.name: Maxwell Food Centre
items.knownFor: Hainanese chicken rice, fish soup, rojak
items.hours: Busiest 11:30am–2pm; most stalls from morning to evening
items.closed: Some stalls close one day a week; periodic cleaning closures
text: The obvious first stop, a short walk from Chinatown MRT. The famous chicken rice stalls have queues at lunch; go at 10:30am or after 2pm.

items.name: Chinatown Complex Food Centre
items.knownFor: Claypot rice, roast meats, dim sum, craft beer
items.hours: Morning to late evening, stall by stall
items.closed: Periodic cleaning closures for the whole centre
text: The largest hawker centre in Singapore, above the wet market. Walk a full lap before choosing.

items.name: Amoy Street Food Centre
text: Fills with office workers from noon. Come at 11:30am or after 1:30pm.

items.name: Tiong Bahru Market
items.knownFor: Chwee kueh, lor mee, pau, kopi
items.hours: Best from early morning to late morning
items.closed: Some stalls rest on Mondays; periodic cleaning closures
text: The breakfast centre. Many stalls sell out or close by early afternoon.

items.name: Tekka Centre
items.knownFor: Biryani, thosai, mutton soup, fresh juice
items.hours: Morning to evening, busiest late morning
items.closed: Stall rest days vary; periodic cleaning closures
text: Food stalls wrap the ground-floor wet market. The biryani queues tell you where to go.

items.name: Lau Pa Sat
items.knownFor: Satay (evenings, on the street outside), Hokkien mee
items.hours: Long hours; satay street from the evening
items.closed: Rarely closed; satay street depends on the day
text: A Victorian cast-iron market hall in the financial district. The satay grills set up on Boon Tat Street in the evening, earlier at weekends.

items.name: Old Airport Road Food Centre
items.knownFor: Char kway teow, lor mee, satay bee hoon, rojak
text: A favourite with locals and a short ride from Katong. Many of its stalls are considered among the best for their dish.

items.name: East Coast Lagoon Food Village
text: Open-air, by the beach, with a sea breeze. Best for an early dinner at sunset.

items.name: Adam Road Food Centre
text: Ten minutes from the Botanic Gardens. A good breakfast after a dawn walk.

items.name: Changi Village Hawker Centre
items.knownFor: Nasi lemak, satay bee hoon, fresh juices
text: Beside the Pulau Ubin ferry and ten minutes from the airport.

items.name: Golden Mile Food Centre
items.knownFor: Army stew, Malay and Thai stalls, ondeh ondeh
text: A short walk from Kampong Glam, less visited by tourists.

items.name: Newton Food Centre
text: Famous and photogenic, and the one place where we suggest checking prices before you order seafood sold by weight.

centres.note: **Cleaning closures:** every hawker centre closes for a few days of cleaning several times a year, and some for longer renovations. The National Environment Agency publishes the schedule. Stall hours change, and hawkers take holidays, especially around Chinese New Year and Hari Raya. Check before you cross town for a single stall.

manners.title: Four habits that make you look like a regular
manners.text: Nobody will mind if you get these wrong. But they are part of the culture UNESCO recognised, and doing them right makes the hall work better for everyone.

items.title: Chope a seat
items.text: A packet of tissues on a table means it is taken: someone has 'choped' it and gone to order. Do not move it. If you are a group, one person holds the table while the others queue; if you are alone, share a table with a nod.

items.title: Queue for one dish
items.text: Each stall does one thing well. Order at several stalls, tell them your table number if there is one, and pay at each. Many take cards and QR payments now, but carry some cash for older stalls.

items.title: Return your tray
items.text: Since 2021, returning trays and crockery to the tray-return points has been the rule, not a courtesy. Halal and non-halal return points are separate: use the one matching the stall you bought from.

items.title: Speak the order
items.text: Learn the coffee code: kopi is coffee with condensed milk, kopi-o is black with sugar, kopi-c is with evaporated milk, and kosong means no sugar. Peng means iced. 'Kopi-o kosong peng' is iced black coffee without sugar.

dishes.name: Hainanese chicken rice
text: Poached chicken, rice cooked in chicken stock with ginger and pandan, chilli sauce and dark soy. The unofficial national dish.

dishes.name: Laksa
text: Rice noodles in a spiced coconut curry broth with prawns and cockles. Katong laksa is cut short so you can eat it with a spoon.

dishes.name: Char kway teow
text: Flat rice noodles fried over high heat with dark soy, lard, cockles, Chinese sausage and egg. Smoky, rich, not light.

dishes.name: Nasi lemak
text: Coconut rice with sambal, fried anchovies, peanuts, egg and usually fried chicken. A Malay breakfast that is good at any hour.

dishes.name: Satay
text: Skewers of marinated chicken, mutton or beef grilled over charcoal and served with peanut sauce, cucumber and rice cakes.

dishes.name: Roti prata
text: Flaky griddled flatbread, plain or with egg, with curry for dipping. The late-night snack of choice.

dishes.name: Chwee kueh
text: Soft steamed rice cakes topped with fried preserved radish and chilli. A Tiong Bahru breakfast.

dishes.name: Hokkien mee
text: Yellow noodles and rice vermicelli braised in a rich prawn stock, with a squeeze of lime and sambal.

dishes.name: Biryani
text: Fragrant rice layered with spiced chicken or mutton, best at Tekka Centre in the morning.

dishes.name: Ice kachang
text: Shaved ice over beans, jelly and sweetcorn, drenched in syrups and evaporated milk. The cure for a hot afternoon.

a: Hawker stalls are licensed and inspected, and each displays a hygiene grade. As anywhere, popular stalls with high turnover are a good sign.
Look for stalls marked vegetarian (often Buddhist vegetarian, which also excludes onion and garlic) and the South Indian stalls at Tekka. Ask about fish sauce and lard, which appear in many dishes.
Halal-certified stalls display a certificate. Many Malay and Indian-Muslim stalls are halal; Chinese stalls generally are not unless certified.
No. Most hawker centres are open-sided and cooled by ceiling fans. In the hottest hours, go to centres with good cross-ventilation, or pick a cooler time of day.
